title: Pentecost in red
hookLine: churches wear red, some read Acts in many languages at once

lines: ONE STORY, MANY VOICES AT ONCE.
cards: The reader steps up to the lectern on Pentecost Sunday and starts the story in English. A moment later a second voice joins in, in Spanish. Then a third, in Korean.
A fourth, in Swahili. A fifth, in something nobody in the third row can place. For a few seconds the church is a wonderful mess of sound, some catching their own language somewhere in the noise.
And the room has gone red: red stoles, red banners, people in red shirts and scarves. Some churches do exactly this, on purpose. They're acting out a story.

teach.h: A RUSHING WIND, TONGUES OF FIRE.
teach.b: It's in the second chapter of Acts. Jesus's friends are together in one room, waiting, as they were told.

In the King James Bible: "suddenly there came a sound from heaven as of a rushing mighty wind, and it filled all the house where they were sitting. And there appeared unto them cloven tongues like as of fire, and it sat upon each of them."
That's the red: fire, resting on each person. Then they begin "to speak with other tongues, as the Spirit gave them utterance." The word does double duty.

teach.h: TONGUES ON THEIR HEADS, AND IN THEIR MOUTHS.
teach.b: Tongues of fire on their heads; tongues, meaning languages, in their mouths.

In the street, people from many nations gather, baffled, because "every man heard them speak in his own language." They ask, "how hear we every man in our own tongue, wherein we were born?" Notice what doesn't happen.
The Spirit doesn't hand everyone one shared language. Nobody has to give up their mother tongue to understand.

Some readers hear an answer to the tower of Babel, where languages scattered people: here the languages stay, and people are gathered anyway. Not everybody's impressed. Some mock and say they're "full of new wine."
That's why some churches read Acts in several languages at once on this day: the jumble is the point. And it's why the red.
Acts tells this as the day the Spirit came like fire, and churches that keep the color dress the room to look like it.

how: At Pentecost some churches use red vestments and decorations, and some invite readers to read Acts 2 aloud in several languages at once.

games.q: you're in the street. a crowd is gathering. you hear these people speaking, and it's your own language. what do you ask?
o: how hear we every man in our own tongue?
games.why: the crowd asks "how hear we every man in our own tongue, wherein we were born?" each language is kept, and each is heard.

practice: Hold something red, a sock, a pen, a mug, and let the color stand for the fire in the story. Bring to mind someone whose first language isn't yours, a neighbor, a coworker, and think of the words they grew up with.
If you pray, hold that person before God in their own tongue, without knowing a word of it; if you don't, just honor the language they carry.

wordCard.voice: Glossa. Greek for tongue, meaning language too, the word behind the fire and the many languages the Spirit gave at Pentecost.

orig.note: Greek: tongue, and also language. Acts 2 uses it for both.

carryVoice: Your line: every tongue. Nobody had to give up their own to understand. That's today, done.
